By CD Rose
Here is a book that shows it is possible for a novel to be at once highly original and to fit within an established tradition. But then contradiction is at the heart of the fifth book by British writer CD Rose, and indeed his career – even the titles of some of his earlier works (The Biographical Dictionary of ­Literary Failure; Who’s Who When Everyone is Someone Else) exude a spirit of playful paradox.
We Live Here Now is what Rose calls a “composite novel”: it’s a series of connected stories about the contemporary art world and the people who orbit it. The form makes it both like nothing I’ve read before, and reminiscent of other novels-in-stories by writers such as Italo Calvino and David Mitchell. (I prefer the term by the writer Keith Ridgway, one of the best practitioners of the form, who called it “a shattered novel in a bag”.)
But a book such as this needs a centre to hold it together, otherwise it really is just a collection of stories. With Rose’s novel, the still-point is the work of (fictional) female artist Sigismunda “Sigi” Conrad. The first chapter takes the form of an essay (rejected by the LRB, we’re told) on Conrad’s work, which sounds like Tracey Emin meets Rachel Whiteread: in 2015, Conrad made life-sized rooms, ­collectively titled Where We Live Now. If Conrad’s work is a little predictable, the most interesting thing about her is that she disappeared soon after this exhibition – in ­circumstances only hinted at.
That event sets up the thread of appearances and disappearances that winds through the ensuing 13 chapters, Conrad and her work on the fringes. The contemporary art world is consistently ripe for ­ridicule – “AI would soon do for most of them, thank god”, says one character – and Rose is all too happy to supply. Listen to the art dealer Kasha, who has a cheerfully cynical view of her job: “She’d have loved to work with more emerging artists, she really would, but they weren’t easy to sell to the people she usually worked with who didn’t care if a piece had any integral value of its own.”
Kasha’s story becomes a sort of Kafkaesque chase, as she agrees to source an artwork – presumably a Sigi Conrad piece – for a shadowy buyer she never meets, except via an intermediary with an unpronounceable name. Through her account, the contradictions in the art market are brought to the fore – “art had no value, and could be worth millions” – as are the book’s various disappearances, with the artwork going missing. It’s eventually traced to a freeport in Geneva, a building “all windows, smoked and mirrored”.
From here, the novel’s focus flows outwards. Illogic abounds: one chapter is set on a container ship that may be carrying Kasha’s Conrad artwork, a ship owned by an almost infinitely regressing nest of shell companies, so that “no-one on board really knew who owned the ship” and it was “quite possible not even the owner of the ship knew what they owned either”. This spirit of paradox and contradiction persists when the ship becomes lost – sort of. “Of course we’re not lost,” says one character. “I know where we are. I just don’t know where anything else is.”
Another brings us sound artist Rachel Noyes (note the “noise”, “no/yes”: Rose is an inveterate punster) who gets involved in a Zoom call where no-one can hear anyone else, to be assessed for an arts residency in Berlin that she never applied for. Then there’s Paul, an artist who photographs things then paints over them, who’s commissioned to create a portrait of a business magnate. Paul’s problem is whether he’ll be able to create on canvas the man’s inner life when he doesn’t appear to have one. “I thought I knew what the void was. But then I met Anders Laerp.”
The stories that work best are the ones like those described above, which encase Rose’s more nebulous subjects in a real world gone slightly awry. They feel like something out of sci-fi author M John Harrison’s books, and that’s not the only writer called to mind. There’s a Ballardian interest in non-places, “the corner of the car park, the hard shoulder of a cold and windy road”; a chapter which ends, like Tom McCarthy’s Remainder, with its protagonist endlessly repeating the same journey; even a running joke of made-up car models similar to those in Martin Amis’s Money: the Mercedes Threatener, the Vauxhall Vandal.
But the intensity of Rose’s vision of a world where nothing is what it seems – or rather, where we can’t say for sure – means the book always feels fresh rather than derivative. The range of characters and styles on display means that if you do come across a weaker chapter – that on the man whose identity has been stolen six times, for example – there’ll be another one along soon, such as the one on the drug dealer who finds his cover story of art trading becomes more lucrative for him than the world of illicit substances.
We Live Here Now is both accessible and challenging, entertaining the reader with its ridiculous and sinister figures, even as it prompts more intellectual questions about the reality of appearances. And as the ending demonstrates, questions are far more interesting than answers anyway. “Have we learned anything?” asks one character. “Is that even important?” JS

by Andrev Walden, tr Ian Giles
It takes some confidence to call a book Bloody Awful in Different Ways. Put a foot wrong and the critics already have their headline. But then Andrev Walden’s debut novel isn’t any old debut novel. The 2023 recipient of Sweden’s most prestigious literary award, the August Prize, not to mention the country’s bestselling book across all genres that year, it arrives in Ian Giles’s translation a proven winner.
The novel opens in the run-up to Christmas 1983. Seven-year-old Andrev, who is named after the author and later becomes a writer himself, lives in a tiny Swedish village with his mother, siblings and a man called “the Plant Magician”, known for his habit of eating mushrooms, smoking henbane and administering lavender water enemas. As a Christmas prank, Andrev dresses as Santa and knocks on his own front door, “squeal[ing] with laughter” at the prospect of his family’s laughter. Instead, the Plant Magician hits him. As blood gushes from his face, his mother screams, “He’s not your real dad… A real dad would never do that to his child.”
His real father, his mother reveals, has “long black hair” and “lives in a land far away”, which convinces Andrev that he’s the son of a Native American. It’s “a great thrill – as if an adventure has begun. As if I’m the boy in a book about a boy who finds out his dad is the king of a magical and distant land.” And it is an adventure, of sorts: after the bloody blow, his mum shacks up with one new man after another, giving Andrev the dubious distinction – and the novel the glorious tagline – of being “a boy who has seven fathers in seven years”.
These men present a bleak vision of masculinity. One, unpromisingly known as “the Thief”, ends an argument by pounding Andrev’s mum’s head against the toilet seat. Another, even more unpromisingly known as “the Murderer”, smashes Andrev’s fish tank in a jealous fit of rage at his mother staying out too late. “These bloody men and their violence,” his mum complains. “I don’t know how they find me, but they always do.”
Andrev’s child’s-eye view of this behaviour is observed with heartbreaking acuity. In his first home, he describes how the Plant Magician “likes to administer slaps at the dinner table – quick blows to the back of the head with his open hand – and if you start to cry then he tells you right away that it’s only a slap”, with a blunt factuality – notice the generic “you” – that rings true to the ways abuse victims normalise their experience. His intense gratitude for when “the Plant Magician is full of regret and his hands become soft” might even be seen as a form of Stockholm syndrome: “On days like that I can love him.”
Happily the novel is as funny as it is tragic. To begin with, the comedy is driven by Andrev’s misapprehensions, such as when he mistakes the term “ladies’ man” for a “mythical animal … a blend of woman and man”; or when he supposes that the Plant Magician’s clenched-fist shouts of President Allende’s surname to a Chilean friend is simply how people greet each other in Chile.
As Andrev enters his teens, it becomes more a comedy of embarrassment. In a darkly funny scene, his mum takes him to the doctors, where he’s informed there is something wrong with his foreskin: “I look at the doctor’s desk. If I stand up and headbutt the edge of the desk as hard as possible, it should kill me.” Later, on his first shift as a dishwasher, he’s slow-clapped by an entire restaurant after he accidentally smashes 77 glasses (the numerical precision makes this all the funnier).
Great credit must go to Giles’s translation. The key to humour is timing and that’s easily lost in another language. Not so here. There’s a real snap to the sentences; the punchlines fall just where they need to; and the comic possibilities afforded by punctuation and paragraphing are well exploited. I draw your attention to the moment when one of the fathers stops giving Andrev presents:
“He writes that I’ve got too big for presents and that I probably feel that too.
I don’t.”
But the coup of the book is its take on coming of age. From Andrev’s joy at getting adult humour for the first time (during an episode of Moonlighting), to his resentment at his parents’ happiness (“I usually like it when she laughs, but I don’t like this”), this novel is at once tough and tender. It tells you things about growing up that you didn’t realise were true, not until Walden put them into words.
Comparisons will inevitably be drawn with another Swedish novel, Fredrik Backman’s A Man Called Ove (2012). Similarly perceptive of human behaviour (albeit about an old man rather than a young one) and as tragicomic, that novel went from being Sweden’s bestselling book of 2013 to global blockbuster. There’s no reason why Bloody Awful in Different Ways can’t do the same. Bloody awful? Bloody brilliant, more like. GC
Bloody Awful in Different Ways is published by Penguin at £14.99. To order your copy for £12.99, call 0330 173 0523 or visit Telegraph Books
by Toby Vieira
It is possible we are not quite ready for a book about a pandemic. But if pathogens, testing swabs, and incubation periods must be introduced to contemporary literature, it might be done in the way of The Undrowned, the confident second novel from Toby Vieira. Here, symptoms will feel rather familiar but the writer is careful not to linger on them. Instead, general illness – exhaustion, flu, insomnia – forms the bedrock of a thoroughly modern thriller.
The novel follows British journalist Seb, dispatched to investigate civil unrest in “The Land Of”: a poverty-stricken, post-colonial enclave somewhere in West Africa. Surrounded by mangroves and accessible only by boat, it also seems to be ground-zero of some rapidly mutating virus. Within the opening pages, one of Seb’s three companions goes missing. He’s only vaguely aware of the loss, remembering “lights and noise and stretchers and being given some sort of jab in the arm”.
But he recovers and returns to The Land Of, where Nikki, his second companion, resolves to photograph a crowd of local people. There’s a surge of bodies and then she’s gone. Seb’s third companion, David, vanishes too. Not long afterwards, Seb returns to London, haunted by a conversation in which Nikki said that she had heard knocking at night. Back home, Seb starts to hear the knocking, too; but his employer is nonplussed and the police disinterested. Our hero, it seems, has become a sort of medical curiosity after getting close to the virus – something that attracts the attention of both government officials and menacing, syringe-wielding nurses.
The Undrowned is a pacy and assured novel. Its earlier sections recall Graham Greene; there’s plenty of Joseph Conrad’s influence here, too (and Conrad’s acolytes, with a nod, perhaps, to Apocalypse Now, in a suit “luminescent like napalm”). Seb’s thoughts are “dark swirls”, reminiscent of Eliot’s Prufrock, excerpted in the book’s epigraph. That literary ambition stretches to a dog named Wystan, after Auden.
And yet despite the allusions, The Undrowned is not a period piece. The book is set firmly in the present day – characters check their phones, read online news and brandish plastic NHS badges. A contemporary adventurousness abounds, with Seb bouncing from nation to nation via twin-prop planes, fishing boats, black cabs. It’s a yearning, perhaps, for the smart, comradely world of Vieira’s influences. As for Vieira himself, his biography is brief apart from a detail of him moving across “the UK, France, Switzerland and Belgium, inter alia”. This internationalism might explain his anonymity, or it might be a mischievous bit of elision between text and writer.
That biographical slipperiness becomes particularly apt as the story develops, and Seb becomes more self-estranged. Seb’s three companions, presumed dead, later emerge again, only to be destroyed in “explosions” or “red and yellow” flames. These second deaths, if that’s what they are, mean Seb becomes a suspect for their murders. But more crucially they seem to mark a general breakdown in our protagonist’s life; we start to move from a conventional narrative to something more unstable, as Seb’s grip on reality becomes less and less clear. His flat, we’re told, is repeatedly broken into by men wearing outfits reminiscent of a “Chernobyl clean-up crew”; his mother’s house seems to be entirely submerged in floodwater. Increasingly, we hear descriptions of his dreams. His subconscious, once eddying beneath, becomes the primal force of the novel.
Perhaps this all sounds very exciting. The character’s journeys to the “Zigzag Mountains”, via “rusty steamer” and “long trips by 4x4” certainly are. Somehow, though, not very much happens in The Undrowned, or rather its briskness is such that grand journeys – between London and “the Ethiopian side of the border”, say – run, disappointingly, to only a paragraph. And by wearing his influences so heavily, certain choices appear almost affectedly quaint – his mother’s house is named “Palaver’s End”, while youths are described as “nincompoops”.
Still, Vieira confidently transplants the exploits of a mid-century hero to the current moment, and with it reveals something impressively desolate. This might be the first piece of art that deals deftly with the idea of a pandemic without recalling something unbearable. Instead, The Undrowned shows a different kind of isolation – one that occurs most disconcertingly from the self. SD
The Undrowned is published by Weatherglass at £12.99. To order your copy for £10.99, call 0330 173 0523 or visit Telegraph Books
by Michael Clune
Fifteen-year-old Nick has been kicked out by his mother. He lives with his father in a ramshackle housing development in Illinois: the older man is largely absent, both physically and emotionally. One day in geometry class, Nick suddenly realises that his hand is a thing. “Hand, textbook, eraser. Three things.” He’s at once hyper aware of, but dislocated from, his body; he forgets how to breathe. His vision begins to tunnel. Then he’s back in the room, this brief crisis having been observed only by his friend, Ty, who shakes his head and turns back to his book. “The idea that I was crazy and he was evil was the background joke of our friendship.”
So begins Michael Clune’s deeply impressive first novel, Pan, which explores subjects first discussed in his autobiographical works: White Out (2013; republished by McNally Editions, 2023) and Gamelife: A Memoir (2015). Both are keen studies of childhood, and later, the dissociative psyche of the adolescent.
These previous books, then, have sown the seeds of the most fruitful territory in Pan: after the classroom incident, another episode shortly follows. Nick has just started reading Walter Scott’s Ivanhoe when he becomes aware that something is wrong, which he recalls matter-of-factly: “I was having or was about to have a heart attack.” He plugs on, hoping that he can read his way out of things:
I suspended the heart attack in Ivanhoe. Like when you shake a bottle of oil-and-vinegar salad dressing. As long as you shake the bottle, the oil is suspended in the vinegar. When you stop shaking it, the oil comes out. So long as I read Ivanhoe my heart attack stayed suspended in the story.
He finishes the book in the early hours of the morning, at which point he calmly requests to be taken to the emergency room. There, he is told that his heart is fine; what he has experienced is panic. Pan then follows Nick over the course of a year, as he seeks to understand his newly fractured state of being. He stops sleeping: “I glanced around fearfully at the shadowy shapes of the things in my bedroom. The rumpled pile of my jeans, my shirt. Bulk of the dresser. The knob of the door, like an animal bone. These things, I thought, are asleep. They are asleep right now. That could be me, I thought. That’s what I was about to be.”
One doctor tells him to buy some paper bags to breathe in, before a second diagnoses him with Generalised Anxiety Disorder, for which there is no cure, just therapy. The therapist, in turn, suggests guided meditation, which doesn’t land well. Instead, Nick drifts – or perhaps is pulled – through a series of cultural awakenings. (A cruel irony for an insomniac, perhaps.)
Led by Sarah – with whom he has a not-quite on, not-quite off relationship – he finds himself reading Wilde’s Salome, listening to a recording of Bach’s Orchestral Suites, and confronting Bellini’s Portrait of Doge Leonardo Loredan. As Nick’s psychic landscape becomes turbulent, these revelations become roughly interlinked in his mind, as though stitched together with a shaking hand. In a painting by Giotto, for example, he becomes fixed not on the subject, but a hue: “Red. A very particular red. The red, in fact, of the cover of the Signet Classics edition of Ivanhoe.”
It isn’t an easy task, recreating the thought-processes of a paranoid and adolescent mind, but Clune is remarkably adept at retaining narrative and tonal control. Some scenes have a sense of true eeriness, as when Nick recounts a moment of reverie involving a classmate, feeling “like I could dive out of my face, leave the empty vibrating board of my head behind. Like my looking could drip onto the porous yellow tile of the lunchroom wall, or pour into Nicole’s eyes, into the capacious strangeness of her thoughts, the rooms she knew.”
What time Nick does not spend spacing out in his tedious job at Ace Hardware, he spends in a disused barn on the outskirts of town, with Ty, Sarah, and a new group of outcasts, led by Ian, a college junior who appears to perceive Nick in deep and inexplicable ways. (“Can you wonder now? Can’t you see that the fear of sleep is rational?”) In time, though, Ian’s presence shifts gradually from cool and aloof into something altogether more sinister. It all culminates in a frantic yet enigmatic conclusion, which lingers in the nerve endings for some time.
Clune’s first foray into fiction holds great promise. While there are some longueurs, and an alienated affect that might begin to grate some readers as the novel moves along, he’s a writer of great intensity and imagination; and Pan takes an old conceit – the disturbed-teen Bildungsroman – then crafts it into something strange, wild, unique. GB
Pan is published by Vintage at £16.99. To order your copy for £14.99, call 0330 173 0523 or visit Telegraph Books
by Thomas McMullan
Abandoning society to live in the woods can go one of two ways. You may connect with nature, reassess your priorities and arrive at a deeper understanding of the world you left behind, as Henry David Thoreau did in his cabin by Walden Pond. Or you may end up harassed, haunted and murdered, as in hundreds of horror films.
Thomas McMullan’s frustrating second novel, Groundwater, tries to have it both ways. Liz and John, a young couple from London, have just moved into a remote cottage by a lake. They have come seeking “a harmony with nature, a closeness”, but not for any of the usual reasons. After two years of trying for a baby, their hope is that it will boost their fertility.
They haven’t yet finished unpacking when Liz’s maddeningly fertile sister Monica, her arrogant husband Harrie and their two young children come to stay for the August bank-holiday weekend. Things soon become tense. When the group gets lost on a walk, Harrie reassures them that he knows the way with such “cheerful domination” – “Don’t worry, I have a cognitive map” – that John is cowed into silence. Later, on a trip to a nearby swimming pool, Monica entrusts her children to Liz to put the latter “through her paces”, remarking with glee when one runs off: “It’s not easy keeping on top of them.”
Nor are this brood the only unwanted visitors. Jim Sweet is the local warden, and seems appropriately named when he first drops by, welcoming the young couple to the area with a gift of garden compost. But then he keeps dropping by, to the point where a naked swim in the lake is spoiled by the worry that he might appear again. The same happens with a group of students they befriend: soon the bunch are coming over uninvited and causing merry hell.
All the elements are in place for something truly horrifying; and, as Groundwater unfolds, there are some well-drawn moments of violence. But they’re only moments. With their passing, everything resets; McMullan’s tension, so carefully worked up, is squandered. It’s as though he didn’t know what he wanted the novel to be. Sometimes, for instance, John looks at the woods around him with “a tightness in his chest” and “a dizzying sense that he was not unseen”; other times, those same woods seem wholly benign, even bucolic.
The tonal uncertainty extends to the novel’s setting. To begin with, McMullan is coy about the when and the where, making oblique references to “unprecedented fire conditions” and people dying in their thousands. To this air of dystopia, he adds notes of fairy tale, with Liz and John’s cottage likened to a “gingerbread house” and the area to an “ancient kingdom”. But no: as soon as the students start debating the merits of Keir Starmer and Jeremy Corbyn, any sense of mystery vanishes. We’re in that boring old thing, the real world.
This is all disappointing, coming as it does from the author of 2020’s Betty Trask Prize-winning The Last Good Man. That novel was genuinely dystopian, and while it had its faults – a rather effortful allegory about social media among them – it was at least tonally consistent, with a sustained escalation of tension that built to something memorable. I read Groundwater a few weeks ago, and I’m already forgetting it.
The novel scores better when it attempts to be a relationship drama. In a moment free of visitors, Liz and John try and fail to have sex, the act having become to them a passionless act of procreation. At another point, they succeed, which convinces Liz so firmly that she’s pregnant that she thinks of telling her sister: “She could feel the possibility inside her, a growing sac that would push her outwards, do things to her bones and her veins that she couldn’t yet comprehend.”
Their desperation is heartbreaking – until it becomes ridiculous. “This place was theirs and it would be their child’s too. I am not one thing ageing but forever renewed, [John] thought, the green and the light, the shoots forever reaching, my knees against my chest in the hollow of a tree, ready at a moment’s notice to burst forth.” What is he, an Ent? This novel, I reckoned, would make no less sense if he were. GC
Groundwater is published by Bloomsbury at £18.99. To order your copy for £16.99, call 0330 173 0523 or visit Telegraph Books
by Ferdinand Mount
“Write what you know,” as the old adage goes. Ferdinand Mount, previously the head of the No 10 Policy Unit under Marg­aret Thatcher and a former editor of the Times Literary Supplement, drew on his past lives for the political and journalistic aspects of his last novel, Making Nice (2021). Let’s hope he was merely inventing the book’s hapless protagonist, Dickie Pentecost, who, after joining a dubious PR firm, finds himself out of his depth amid spads, spin and corruption.
In Mount’s latest novel, his 13th, Dickie makes a welcome return. The Pentecost Papers is another sharp satire – this time on the ultra-rich – as well as another exuberant caper. Or as Dickie puts it at the ­outset, it’s “an ill-starred odyssey through an incurably slippery world, and one recorded by several hands – most of them unsteady”.
Making Nice saw Dickie drawn into the orbit of the enigmatic ­pub­li­city chief Ethel (“short for Ethel­bert”), and tasked with ghostwriting the autobiography of an MP. On this occasion, he’s beguiled by an equally elusive figure, named Timothy Smith. Dickie, having ­ret­urned to his former career as a ­diplomatic correspondent, meets “Timbo” on a golf course and by the end of their round regards him as a man of mystery: not only is Timbo engaged in cryptic risk-­management at the shadowy Ophion House, but he’s also possessed of healing hands that assuage Dickie’s backache.
A friendship is forged, and later widened to include Luke Deverill, a bibulous and lecherous cryptographer, and his no-nonsense wife, Lee Thorold. When the troubled ­timber billionaire George Furcht arrives on the scene, Timbo and the married couple set out to discover who is masterminding a ­conspiracy to destroy Furcht’s business and why.
Timbo’s investigations take him to Brazil, where Furcht has been buying up and tearing down swathes of rainforest. But eventually foul play ensues, involving a mocked-up death and a vanishing act. Dickie, who wanted nothing to do with Timbo’s “crackbrained enterprise”, is forced to leave his comfort zone and fly to South America to retrace his friend’s steps. As he ventures further up the Amazon, he wonders whether the sinister cabal intent on bankrupting Furcht might be fanatical enough to resort to murder.
Mount keeps us absorbed by steadily thickening his plot. It’s no great spoiler to reveal that an operation to short the stocks of a logging magnate is only part of the story. Mount’s heroes must also, for instance, grapple with the significance of “green hedges”, and weigh up the intentions of the wealthy and ruthless Sir Wilfrid Bentliff.
The Pentecost Papers serves up a number of lively scenes, from a fashion show in London to a horse race in Paris. But the characters’ journeys in the Brazilian wilderness prove the most compelling: Dickie sails upriver into the heart of darkness, Timbo flees downriver in search of sanctuary. One of the book’s most entertaining set-pieces is its climactic showdown, in which the villain invites Luke and a heavily pregnant Lee to his Yorkshire pile and lectures them on evolution and extinction over a lunch of offal and a terrine of trotters.
All that mars this scene is the length of the discourse. Elsewhere, similarly overlong speeches explain plans or summarise courses of action. At such junctures, I wished that Mount had reduced his thick chunks of exposition to more bite-sized portions. One episode, in which a character makes a great escape from Brazil by using “what this country is really famous for” (clue: not coffee or samba), threatens to turn the novel into a mere farce.
Fortunately, the book’s faults are few. There’s wit, drama and intrigue in abundance here, and the dis­parate plot strands are woven together to constitute a satisfying conclusion. Mount’s cast are drawn with plenty of colour. We meet bit-parters such as Bric, who’s thought to be a White Russian princess but is actually a pharmacist’s daughter from Odesa (“but we lived very close to the Dolgoruky Palace”). More prominent players include Rowley Beavan, a “clapped-out City hack” used to “telling a tale, and tickling it up a bit, too”. But the most captivating character is Timbo. Mount manages to render him both a forceful, blundering presence and “as sinuous and evanescent as a streak of oil on a pond”.
At the beginning, Dickie tells us that “this story is mostly about ­getting it wrong”. His creator ­frequently gets it right. The Pentecost Papers is a hugely enjoyable comedy of manners. If Mount gives Dickie another outing, I can only hope that Timbo comes along for the ride. MF
The Pentecost Papers is published by Bloomsbury at £18.99. To order your copy for £16.99, call 0330 173 5030 or visit Telegraph Books
by Tehila Hakimi
Tehila Hakimi, 43, originally trained as a mechanical engineer. Since 2013, when she began writing, her poetry and short fiction have been widely praised in her native Israel. Now we have Hunting in America, her debut novel, translated from Hebrew by Joanna Chen. It’s a shame, then, to find it a slog. The issue isn’t the book’s length – only 208 pages – but its mood: unvaryingly gloomy and humourless.
The story follows an unnamed Israeli narrator of about the author’s age, who moves from Tel Aviv to America for work. She works for an Israeli company in a boring and stressful job, which requires her to spend her days writing emails and handling clients. She lives alone in a house that has been furnished by her company; at weekends, she generally does nothing at all.
In fact, she seems barely to have any internal life. She doesn’t long for Israel or anyone there. When she realises she has missed a couple of telephone calls from a friend, she doesn’t bother ringing back, as she assumes that the call was a mistake. Months later, when her mother calls for a chat, the narrator is so repelled by the sound of her voice that she holds the mobile at a distance from her ear, like a stroppy teenager.
This eerie, dreary life is enlivened, however – if only a little – by hunting trips on which the narrator goes with a colleague, David. He is married and a few years older than her; he takes a paternalistic interest in her from the start, teaching her, for instance, how to skin deer, and which parts of their bodies to aim for while shooting to ensure that they die fast. We soon learn that the narrator spent time in the IDF, and she still knows how to handle a gun. David notices she’s a natural, but treats her with condescension anyway – and rather than find this annoying, the narrator seems to relish it.
Hakimi’s story is structured around a dozen or so of these trips, sometimes taken with David and other colleagues, sometimes by the narrator alone. Gradually, she and David fall into a liaison of sorts, under the blankly benevolent eye of his wife Miriam. At the same time, trouble begins brewing at work, and gradually we learn about the events in Israel that led the narrator to want to bin her old life and start afresh.
Hunting in America reminded me of Ottessa Moshfegh’s 2018 novel My Year of Rest and Relaxation. It has a wilfully flat effect. If our heroine has a dominant personality trait, it’s listlessness; but, beyond her passion for hunting, there’s not much else to her. It could be that Hakimi is trying to articulate, through her narrator, the way that modern life flattens the individual. Fine: but it’s dispiriting to have to spend time with this woman, who never has an interesting thought and just drifts about, letting things happen to her.
There are, of course, mopey people out there in the world. But they tend to be the sort of people that the non-mopey majority take pains to avoid. It’s a pity finding such a high concentration of them in these pages. David, the narrator’s colleague, is also a drag; so is Miriam. And the reader is forced to spend long stretches perched on the narrator’s shoulder as she navigates stressful times at work: tense conversations with her boss, a looming restructuring, and so on. It’s all plausibly described, but to what end? In general, we read fiction to escape the tedium of the office, not marinate in it.
There are, occasionally, moments in which Hakimi’s writing makes the juice feel worth the squeeze. The scenes set in Israel, before the narrator’s departure for America, are intriguing: we see snatches of her large family, the bustling life she has chosen to reject. The night before she leaves the country, a bomb falls nearby, and she jokes that it must be Hamas bidding her farewell. Just before the flight, she lingers for a moment on the pavement outside the airport. As usual, she notes, there’s something “like a carcass” in the Israeli summer air. LA

by Susan Choi
Flashlight, the engrossing sixth novel by the American writer Susan Choi, opens with Louisa and her father making their way down a breakwater at the tail end of a Japanese sunset. Louisa’s mother is absent: she “isn’t well”. Her father, who holds a flashlight in one hand and Louisa’s hand in the other, confesses that he has never learned to swim: “I grew up a poor boy. I had no YMCA.” He tells Louisa to “act thankful now” to her mother for making her learn. And, Choi, writes, “those are the last words he ever says to her. (Or are they the last words that she can remember? Did he say something more? There is no one to ask.)” He vanishes into the water. No body is ever found.
Fans of Choi’s work – which delights in playing with the reader’s expectations – may remember the set up. This prelude was first published four years ago as a short story, also called Flashlight. At the time, Choi talked about “wrestling with this material… trying to figure out what it wants to be – a short novel, or a long novel, or stories, or one story”. Her 447-page, six-part, sprawling family epic, which takes in five countries, spans several decades, and is mostly written in a free-indirect style that allows Choi to switch between four main characters, is her answer.
The narrative proper begins with Louisa’s father. It’s spring 1945; he’s six years old. His parents are Korean exiles, who left their homeland, Jeju island, for Japan, and while his Japanese name is Hiroshi, at home he is Seok. Later, when he emigrates to the US on a graduate visa, he goes by Serk. (Shifting identities are a running theme in Choi’s work, not least in her last novel, Trust Exercise, a bestseller that won the 2019 National Book Award.) Next, we meet Anne, Louisa’s mother, who has abandoned her family and her chances of a high school diploma for a man who abandons her once she becomes pregnant. She is forced to give up the baby, Tobias – after a vivid labour “where the vengeance of God tore her entrails out by the roots” – but he will re-emerge later as a pivotal character.
Novels developed from a short story are legion: Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway, Jonathan Franzen’s The Corrections, Haruki Murakami’s The Wind-Up Bird Chronicles, Charles Baxter’s Saul and Patsy. But in freeing their writer from length restrictions, novels pose a counter-challenge: can a writer justify the many tangents of their narrative? Choi stripped most of the backstory out of her original story leaving her with plenty of gaps to fill in. Is Louisa’s mother ill? Why did her father make them leave the US, and Louisa’s fourth grade, for a sabbatical in Japan? And what is the significance of her father’s flashlight?
Choi takes too long to get to the meat of her story: what happened, or will happen, to Serk? Less patient readers may stop. But it pays to persevere. Choi is an astute, convincing writer, whose prose bristles with vivid imagery. In that opening section, 10-year-old Louisa lies in bed while “the dark slid itself onto her chest like a snake, organising its weight into nearly stacked coils that might go on forever and bury her, crush her, if she didn’t leap out of bed just in time.” Choi’s choppy rhythm conveys a child’s breathless angst.
If Trust Exercise was about who controls a story, then Flashlight is about what happens when your own story is out of control. Louisa spends her life dealing with the aftermath of her father’s supposed drowning. A child psychologist reminds her that she told the person who found her that her father had been kidnapped. “No I didn’t,” she retorts – the reality of what happened to them remaining a riddle for most of the novel.
The book’s title, Flashlight, is a metaphor that works hard throughout, illuminating certain events while keeping others in the dark. Serk doesn’t know about Anne’s son; Anne doesn’t know about Serk’s Korean heritage. The flashes of understanding that occur to characters as the decades roll by are like shapes that emerge from the gloom when someone sweeps a torch beam to and fro. And ultimately, the light Choi shines on an astonishing international scandal – revealed in the “Acknowledgements” section for those who want to skip ahead – makes Flashlight a rewarding read. The expansion was well worth it. SM
